title: A Hundred Stones: Berthon from the rue Vavin to the Register at Sceaux
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Villefranche-sur-Saone, the birth on the fifteenth of March
stops.date_confidence: Attested. Wikidata Q2178796 and fr.wikipedia agree on 15 March 1872 at Villefranche-sur-Saone, and en.wikipedia gives the same birth date and place, so the language editions differ only over the death. Wikidata's English description string says born in Chartrettes, which contradicts its own referenced statement P19, Villefranche-sur-Saone, and belongs to another man; it is ignored here.
stops.campa: In the Beaujolais town on the Saone a son is born to an inspector of primary education and entered in the register as Paul Louis Joseph Berthon. The father's work is the state's work: to walk into schoolrooms across the department and judge how children are taught to read, to reckon, and to draw. Drawing is the third of those, and in the France of 1872 it is a national industry as much as an accomplishment, the discipline that supplies pattern to looms, presses, and porcelain. The boy will spend his whole life inside that third subject.
suggested_refs: Wikidata Q2178796, statement P19, place of birth Villefranche-sur-Saone

stops.name: Villefranche-sur-Saone, the first lessons in paint
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. en.wikipedia states that he studied painting in his home town before going to Paris, and gives no year, no teacher, and no institution. 1885 is a placeholder inside his boyhood, chosen only to hold the sequence ahead of the 1893 Paris enrollment, and attests nothing.
stops.campa: He learns to paint here, in the town he was born in, before anyone in Paris has heard of him. No source names the master, the room, or the year. What survives is only the order of things: paint first, and the flat ornamented line long afterwards, so that the posters he draws in his twenties are made by a hand trained on modelling and shadow. The Beaujolais keeps nothing else of him. When the record resumes he is already twenty-one years old and living on the left bank of the Seine.
suggested_refs: Municipal drawing instruction in the Rhone departement in the 1880s, unidentified for this subject

segments.name: The School on the rue Vavin

stops.name: Paris, the school that trained designers, not teachers
stops.date_confidence: From 1893, attested by fr.wikipedia; the month is unknown and defaults to January. Coordinates corrected: the Ecole normale d'enseignement du dessin, the Ecole Guerin founded in 1881, stood at 19 rue Vavin and 9 rue Brea in the sixth arrondissement, approximately 48.8435 north and 2.3298 east. An earlier pass placed it at 48.85 and 2.345, about 1.3 km away near the Ile de la Cite, and called it the state school for training drawing teachers; it was a private school for industrial designers.
stops.campa: He comes up to Paris and enrolls in a school whose name promises a teachers' college and whose business is something else: a private academy on the rue Vavin, founded twelve years earlier, that trains designers for industry. Its pupils learn ornament as a trade, the composition of a wallpaper, a tile, a printed page. Berthon arrives wanting to be a painter. He has walked into the one building in Paris where the decorative arts are taught as a career and not as a demotion, and he will never work outside them again.
suggested_refs: The Ecole normale d'enseignement du dessin, known as the Ecole Guerin, 19 rue Vavin and 9 rue Brea, Paris 6e

stops.name: Paris, rue Vavin, the painting masters
stops.date_confidence: Merson as painting master is attested by en.wikipedia and fr.wikipedia; Puvis de Chavannes at the same school by fr.wikipedia and de.wikipedia. Neither source dates the individual classes. June 1893 stands for the first school year and carries no weight beyond that.
stops.campa: For painting he is put under Luc-Olivier Merson, the prix de Rome man whose sphinxes and flights into Egypt hang in the Salon and whose drawing will later be printed on French postage and on the hundred-franc note. Puvis de Chavannes teaches here too, pale wall painting stripped of incident. Between them Berthon is handed the whole authority of the mural tradition, the figure held still against a flat ground. He keeps the flatness for the rest of his life and throws away everything the two of them meant it to carry.
suggested_refs: luc_olivier_merson.journey.json, the atlas journey of his painting master

stops.name: Paris, rue Vavin, the chair of decorative composition
stops.date_confidence: Grasset's decisive influence is attested convergently by en, fr, and de.wikipedia. He held the chair of decorative composition at this school from 1891 to 1903, so the instruction sits securely inside Berthon's years there, but no source dates the classes; 1895 is a midpoint and is reconstruction.
stops.campa: Eugene Grasset holds the chair of decorative composition in the same building. Grasset is Swiss, a designer of typefaces and stained glass and the flowered plate, and he teaches ornament drawn from the living plant, the stem obeyed rather than prettified. Berthon takes it whole. The Salon painting he came to Paris for quietly stops being the point. What he wants now is a printed surface, editioned by the hundred, sold cheap and pinned to somebody's wall by people who will never own a picture.
stops.quote: had a far greater influence on him, and he may be regarded as his pupil
suggested_refs: Eugene Grasset, chair of decorative composition at the Ecole Guerin, 1891 to 1903

stops.name: Paris, rue Vavin, the year the imitation thins
stops.date_confidence: Attested with the sources' own approximation: de.wikipedia puts the break with direct imitation of Grasset around 1896, and fr.wikipedia's stylistic comparison is dated vers 1896. The month is unknown and defaults to January.
stops.campa: For a while his work is Grasset's work at one remove, close enough that French Wikipedia files him beside another pupil of the same room, Maurice Pillard Verneuil, as a young man whose first things look like the master's. Around 1896 the resemblance thins. The women stay, the flowers stay, the outline stays; what enters is a slower and heavier stem, and a palette of moss and dust that belongs to nobody else. He is twenty-four, and he has found the surface he will work for the rest of the century.
stops.quote: Tout comme Maurice Pillard Verneuil, les premières œuvres de Paul Berthon (vers 1896) montrent un style proche de celui de Grasset.
suggested_refs: Maurice Pillard Verneuil, fellow pupil of Grasset, named in fr.wikipedia's comparison

stops.name: Paris, the Champ-de-Mars, furniture and bindings at the Salon
stops.date_confidence: The fact of exhibiting furniture designs and book bindings at the Salon of 1895 is attested by fr.wikipedia, which names no venue and no month. The venue is reconstruction: applied and decorative art in 1895 was shown by the Societe nationale des beaux-arts at the Palais du Champ-de-Mars, approximately 48.8556 and 2.2986, not at the Palais de l'Industrie as an earlier pass assumed while tagging the item attested.
stops.campa: Before a single poster of his is pasted anywhere he shows furniture and bound books. This is the order Grasset's teaching produces: the chair and the binding first, the affiche after, all of them the same problem of covering a surface without lying about what lies under it. The Salon of 1895 takes the young man's cabinetwork and his leather. No source names the pieces and no photograph of them has been traced. What survives of that year is that he was in the room.
suggested_refs: Societe nationale des beaux-arts, Salon of 1895, Palais du Champ-de-Mars

stops.name: Paris, 31 rue Bonaparte, the Salon des Cent
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction, left open. en.wikipedia dates a Berthon Salon des Cent poster to 1895; fr.wikipedia dates his participation to 1896. The sheet is for exhibition number 17, which falls across the turn of the two years, and neither reading is preferred here. The address, 31 rue Bonaparte, the offices of La Plume, is attested by fr.wikipedia's article on the Salon des Cent.
stops.campa: The review La Plume runs a gallery out of its own offices on the rue Bonaparte and hangs a hundred works at a time, posters among them, priced for people who cannot buy paintings. Berthon shows there and draws the poster for one of the exhibitions, the seventeenth. The Salon des Cent is where the affiche stops being an advertisement stuck to a wall and becomes a print somebody collects, and that difference is exactly the one his own work will depend on: an image with nothing to sell except itself.
suggested_refs: The Salon des Cent at the offices of La Plume, 31 rue Bonaparte, Paris 6e

stops.name: Paris, the Folies Bergere, Liane de Pougy on the wall
stops.date_confidence: Attested by fr.wikipedia's gallery caption, which names both the subject and the year: Liane de Pougy aux Folies Bergere en 1896 par Paul Berthon. de.wikipedia mentions Folies Bergere performers without any date, and an earlier pass reported the whole item as undated. The month is unknown. Coordinates are the theatre at 32 rue Richer in the ninth arrondissement, supplied here rather than taken from a source, and are reconstruction.
stops.campa: The music hall on the rue Richer sells its bill by the wall, and the wall that year carries Liane de Pougy, courtesan and dancer, drawn by Berthon. It is the one commission of his that belongs squarely to the trade the poster was invented for: a named woman, a named house, a date, a thing to come and see. Most of what he makes has no such business in it. He will spend the years after this drawing women who advertise nothing, and the Pougy sheet stands at the edge of his work like a door he chose not to go through.
stops.quote: Liane de Pougy aux Folies Bergère en 1896 par Paul Berthon
suggested_refs: The Folies Bergere, 32 rue Richer, Paris 9e

stops.name: Paris, 31 rue Bonaparte, the drawings for La Plume
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The attribution rests on file metadata in the Wikimedia Commons category for Berthon, which associates illustrations for La Plume with 1895 and 1899; no article text and no printed issue was consulted. 1899 is used for this stop and the 1895 association is folded into the Salon des Cent stop above.
stops.campa: He draws for the review as well as for its gallery. La Plume is the house organ of the poster craze, the place where Cheret and Grasset and Mucha are argued over as artists rather than as tradesmen, and its offices, its gallery, and its printed pages are one address doing three things at once. Berthon's contribution to the pages is known only from the way librarians have catalogued loose sheets. No printed issue has been read against those labels, and the drawings stand on catalogue metadata alone.
suggested_refs: Wikimedia Commons, Category:Paul Berthon, La Plume file metadata

segments.name: Bourgerie, Chaix, and a Hundred Stones

stops.name: Paris, rue Bergere, the presses of Chaix et Cie
stops.date_confidence: The printers are attested by fr.wikipedia: lithographs notably at Bourgerie et Cie, chromolithographs at Chaix et Cie. No date attaches to the relationship and mid-1896 is placed at the opening of his poster decade. Coordinates are the Chaix works in the rue Bergere, ninth arrondissement, approximately 48.8727 and 2.3450; Bourgerie's address is not confirmed in any source reached, so this pin stands for both and is reconstruction.
stops.campa: The stone is the fact under all of it. He draws on limestone at Chaix in the rue Bergere for colour work and at Bourgerie for black, and the print shop decides what the drawing can be: how many stones, how many pulls, how flat the ink must lie to register. His line thickens to carry it. The moss greens and the dead golds are chosen because they will hold on paper at a hundred impressions. Everything the eye later calls his style began as a negotiation with a pressman about what the client would pay for.
suggested_refs: The Chaix works, rue Bergere, Paris 9e; Bourgerie et Cie, address unlocated

stops.name: Paris, the binding for Les Maitres de l'Affiche
stops.date_confidence: January 1897, attested by fr.wikipedia's article on Les Maitres de l'affiche: the albums were relie par Jean Engel d'apres la maquette de Paul Berthon. An earlier pass called this the series cover and dated it 1895, which is impossible, since the series only began publishing in December 1895. Chaix printed the series and the pin is the Chaix works.
stops.campa: Chaix prints the great poster anthology, a plate a month in small format, and at the turn of 1897 the loose sheets are gathered into bound albums. The binding is Jean Engel's work carried out from Berthon's design. He is twenty-four, and before he has a single plate of his own inside the series he has been handed the object itself to dress: the case in which the whole trade will be passed down to collectors. The binder's name goes on it, and his name goes on it beside the binder's.
stops.quote: relié par Jean Engel d'après la maquette de Paul Berthon
suggested_refs: The bound albums of Les Maitres de l'affiche, binding by Jean Engel after Berthon's maquette, January 1897

stops.name: Paris, the hundred sheets and the two thirds
stops.date_confidence: fr.wikipedia alone supports the figure of about a hundred lithographs, chromolithographs, and woodcuts, two thirds of them described as decorative panels. de.wikipedia contradicts it, speaking of hundreds of black-and-white and multicoloured lithographs; an earlier pass wrongly cited both encyclopedias in support of the smaller number. The contradiction is recorded and not adjudicated. The date is a midpoint of the working decade and is not an event.
stops.campa: Count the output and the shape of the career appears. Around a hundred sheets, and two of every three of them not advertisements at all but panneaux decoratifs, decorative panels: a woman, a plant, a border, nothing for sale. He is working the poster's machinery without the poster's purpose, printing pictures for walls in houses where an oil painting is out of reach. Few of his contemporaries choose that trade. Most arrive in it having failed at something more respectable. He chooses it.
stops.quote: une centaine de lithographies (imprimées notamment chez Bourgerie et Cie), de chromolithographies (chez Chaix & Cie) et gravures sur bois, dont deux tiers qualifiées de panneaux décoratifs
suggested_refs: The panneau decoratif as a print genre of the 1890s, distinct from the affiche

stops.name: Paris, plate 175 of the fourth volume
stops.date_confidence: fr.wikipedia's article on the series credits Berthon with plate 175, in volume four, which ran to November 1899; the date given here is the close of that volume and not the day of printing. An earlier pass read a count of thirteen files in the Wikimedia Commons category as thirteen plates, which overstates his participation by a factor of six.
stops.campa: One plate. In five years and two hundred and forty sheets the anthology of the masters of the poster admits him once, at number one hundred and seventy-five, near the end of the fourth volume. The men who fill the rest are the men whose names sell theatres, bicycles, and absinthe. Berthon has spent the decade making pictures that advertise nothing, and the canon of advertising takes him accordingly, once and late. The binding he designed holds more of his work than the contents do.
suggested_refs: Les Maitres de l'affiche, plate 175, volume 4, published to November 1899

stops.name: Paris, plate 227 and the drawings that never reached the stone
stops.date_confidence: fr.wikipedia credits Berthon with plate 227 in volume five, which ran to November 1900, together with drawings made for that volume that were never published. The series itself ended in November 1900. The date is the volume's close, not a day.
stops.campa: A second plate in the fifth and last volume, and then drawings made for that volume that never reach the stone. The series stops in November 1900. Chaix winds it up, the subscribers are released, and whatever Berthon still had in hand goes into a drawer. He is twenty-eight years old. The decade that invented the collectable poster has closed its own account, and the men who lived by it, him among them, are left holding a trade the turning century has quietly finished with.
suggested_refs: Les Maitres de l'affiche, plate 227, volume 5, published to November 1900, with unpublished Berthon drawings

stops.name: Paris, the July cover of L'Image
stops.date_confidence: Attested by fr.wikipedia, which dates the wood-engraved cover for the magazine L'Image to July 1897. The day is unknown and defaults to the first. The publisher's address was not established in any source reached, so the pin is the canonical Paris anchor rather than a located building.
stops.campa: For the July number of L'Image he cuts a cover in wood. The magazine is a wood-engraver's magazine, made by a guild of men reviving a technique that photography had made unnecessary, and the invitation places Berthon among them: not only a lithographer of coloured stones but a man who will take a knife to a block for the sake of a line only a block can give. The same year will carry his name onto a railway hoarding and onto a literary review. He is working at the top of his speed.
suggested_refs: L'Image, July 1897, wood-engraved cover after Berthon

stops.name: Paris, the Gare Saint-Lazare, Normandie-Bretagne
stops.date_confidence: Attested by en.wikipedia and fr.wikipedia: a poster for the Compagnie des chemins de fer de l'Ouest, Normandie-Bretagne, dated 1897. The month is unknown and June is a placeholder. Coordinates anchor the company's Paris terminus district around the Gare Saint-Lazare and are reconstruction; no source places Berthon in Normandy or Brittany, and nothing suggests he travelled to see either.
stops.campa: The Western Railway wants the two provinces at the end of its line made desirable, and Berthon draws them without going. A woman, apple boughs, a coif, the sea reduced to a band of colour: Normandy and Brittany as ornament, produced in a Paris studio a few streets from the terminus the trains actually leave from. It is how the trade works. The poster that sells a journey is made by a man who stays put, and the country in the picture exists on paper before any traveller arrives to check it.
suggested_refs: Compagnie des chemins de fer de l'Ouest, poster Normandie-Bretagne, 1897

stops.name: Paris, the poster for L'Ermitage
stops.date_confidence: 1897, attested, and an earlier error corrected. fr.wikipedia's body text places the L'Ermitage poster in the same year as the L'Image cover and the Normandie-Bretagne poster, and its gallery caption reads 1897; en.wikipedia's gallery also gives 1897, citing LACMA M.87.294.2. An earlier chronology pass dated it 1898 while its own geography lens said 1897. The month is unknown and September is a placeholder.
stops.campa: L'Ermitage is a symbolist review, small and serious, read by a few hundred people who take literature as a vocation, and it wants a wall poster in the way a theatre wants one. Berthon gives it one. The figure is a woman with a book, drawn in the same flattened idiom he uses for railways and violin lessons. He does not change register for a literary client. Poetry and a train to Brittany get the same stem, the same heavy coil of hair, the same three earths of colour.
suggested_refs: Poster for the review L'Ermitage, 1897, LACMA M.87.294.2

stops.name: Paris, the Dutch lady with tulips
stops.date_confidence: Correction rather than contradiction. en.wikipedia captions a Berthon chromolithograph as a portrait of Queen Wilhelmina dated 1898; the file is Dutch Lady with Tulips, which the Boston Public Library catalogues as a chromolithograph published by L. Prang and Company about 1897, and the Wilhelmina identification exists only as a Wikimedia Commons category, not as a museum attribution. Dated about 1897 here after the library record, with June as a placeholder month.
stops.campa: A woman in a Dutch cap among tulips, printed in colour and sold across the Atlantic by a Boston lithographic house that made its fortune on chromos for American parlours. The sheet has been called a portrait of the young queen of the Netherlands by people cataloguing it a century later; the library that holds it calls it nothing of the kind. It is a costume and a flower, which is what his panels almost always are. The nationality in the picture is a decorative property and not a subject.
suggested_refs: Boston Public Library, Dutch Lady with Tulips, chromolithograph, L. Prang and Company, c. 1897

stops.name: Paris, the fifth arrondissement, the marriage of 1898
stops.date_confidence: Attested through a primary record: fr.wikipedia's wikitext cites Archives de Paris, fifth arrondissement, acte de mariage number 641, annee 1898. An earlier pass rated this low-confidence because it arrived through an automated page summary, but the citation is in the article's own source apparatus. Neither the day, the month, nor the bride's name was recovered, so the date defaults to January. Coordinates are the town hall of the fifth arrondissement, where such an act is drawn, and are reconstruction.
stops.campa: He marries in the fifth arrondissement, and the act is number six hundred and forty-one in that year's register. The bride's name has not been read out of the record by anyone whose work was reachable. This is the whole of his private life as it survives: a number in a bound volume in the Paris archives, entered in the middle of his busiest working years, with no letters and no photograph of a household to set beside it. The posters appear at the same rate on either side of it.
suggested_refs: Archives de Paris, 5e arrondissement, acte de mariage n. 641, annee 1898

stops.name: Paris, rue Montparnasse, the Larousse plate
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The only evidence reached is a Wikimedia Commons filename, Paul Berthon - Revue Encyclopedique Larousse 1898.jpg; no catalogue entry and no printed issue was checked, so the earlier attested tag is downgraded here. Coordinates corrected to the historic Librairie Larousse premises at 13 to 21 rue Montparnasse, approximately 48.8443 and 2.3283, some 250 m north of the earlier pin. The month is unknown.
stops.campa: A drawing for the Revue Encyclopedique, published from the Larousse house on the rue Montparnasse. The encyclopedia trade is the other half of the decorative decade, worked by the same presses and the same draughtsmen and just as hungry for an ornamented page, turned to the business of explaining the world alphabetically to a middle class learning to buy reference books. Whether Berthon supplied a cover, a plate, or a headpiece is recorded nowhere reachable. The sheet is known; the commission behind it is not.
suggested_refs: Librairie Larousse, 13 to 21 rue Montparnasse, Paris 6e; Revue Encyclopedique, 1898

stops.name: Paris, the violin lesson and the two dates
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction, left open, with a lean. en.wikipedia dates Lecons de violon to 1895; fr.wikipedia's body text dates it 1898 while fr.wikipedia's own gallery caption dates it 1895, so the split is not cleanly between the two encyclopedias as an earlier pass reported, and de.wikipedia does not mention the work at all and cannot be cited for 1898. External evidence favours the later date: the design is plate 175 of Les Maitres de l'affiche, in a volume that ran to November 1899. 1898 is used as the better supported reading and 1895 is not discarded. The pin is the printers, not a located studio.
stops.campa: A girl, a violin, a wall of stems: the sheet that will end up the best known thing he ever drew. It hangs on the dating question like a coat on a nail. One encyclopedia puts it in 1895, another puts it in 1898 in its text and 1895 in its own picture caption, and the plate number in the poster anthology pulls toward the end of the decade. Nobody has opened the printer's records. A picture reproduced ten thousand times over a century still cannot say in what year its stone was drawn.
suggested_refs: Lecons de violon, Les Maitres de l'affiche plate 175, volume 4

stops.name: Mettlach, the designs sent to Villeroy and Boch
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to place. The collaboration with Villeroy and Boch in the late 1890s is attested by fr.wikipedia and de.wikipedia; no source says Berthon travelled to Mettlach, and designers of the period ordinarily supplied artwork by post. 1898 is a placeholder inside the stated range. Coordinates corrected to the works in the Alte Abtei at Mettlach, about 49.4944 and 6.5978; the earlier pin lay some 2.1 km southwest of the town, in the loop of the Saar.
stops.campa: His ornament crosses a border he probably never crosses himself. The great ceramic house on the Saar takes designs from him for its decorated wares, and the flat outlined plant that was drawn to be pulled on a lithographic press is fired instead onto glaze. It is the ordinary destiny of a pattern in these years: from the stone to the tile, from the poster to the plate, wherever a surface is waiting. Whether a single crate of the finished ware was ever put into his hands is recorded nowhere reachable.
suggested_refs: Villeroy and Boch works, Alte Abtei, Mettlach, Saarland

stops.name: Paris, Phryne before the judges
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The work is dated 1899 in file metadata in the Wikimedia Commons category for Berthon; no museum catalogue entry was checked and the month is unknown. An earlier pass tagged this attested on the strength of a Commons category, which is an attribution and not an attestation.
stops.campa: He draws Phryne, the courtesan of Athens whom the orator stripped before the court so that the judges would acquit a body they could not bring themselves to condemn. In Berthon's hands she is another panel: hair, stem, a band of colour, the antique subject flattened into ornament the same way a railway coast was flattened two years earlier. The decorative art of the century keeps reaching for such names, and keeps making of them the same standing woman. Nothing in the sheet needs the story it is titled after.
suggested_refs: Phryne, 1899, Wikimedia Commons file metadata

stops.name: Paris, Sarah Bernhardt as the distant princess
stops.date_confidence: Attested by en.wikipedia: a lithograph for La Princesse Lointaine featuring Sarah Bernhardt, dated 1901. The month is unknown and defaults to January. The printer and the occasion were not established in any source reached, and no evidence was found that Bernhardt sat for him or commissioned the sheet.
stops.campa: The Princesse Lointaine is Bernhardt's part, and Mucha's poster for her has already settled how the age will draw an actress. Berthon comes to the same subject late and gives it his own treatment: the tragedienne turned into a panel of hair and lily and dulled gold, less an announcement of a performance than an object to hang. It is the last well documented sheet of his career. After it the record of what he made thins out, and it does not recover.
suggested_refs: La Princesse Lointaine, lithograph after Sarah Bernhardt in Rostand's play, 1901

stops.name: Apeldoorn, the queen in the Frisian cap
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to place, and a distinct object from the Boston chromolithograph. A work record linked from Wikidata gives a Berthon portrait of Wilhelmina with a Frisian cap, associated with 1901 and held at the National Museum Paleis Het Loo. No travel to the Netherlands is attested; he worked in Paris, and the pin is the museum that holds the sheet rather than a place he stood. Month unknown.
stops.campa: The young queen of the Netherlands, three years crowned, sits for nobody: the portrait is made in Paris out of costume plates and photographs, and the Frisian cap does the work a coif of Brittany did on the railway poster four years before. The sheet ends up at the palace of Het Loo, in the country of its subject, which is the only sense in which Berthon reaches the Netherlands at all. His pictures travel and the record holds no evidence that the man does.
suggested_refs: National Museum Paleis Het Loo, Portret van Wilhelmina met Friesche muts
sources: Wikidata Q2178796 and the linked work record

stops.name: Paris, the record thins to nothing
stops.date_confidence: A gap, stated as a gap. After the Bernhardt lithograph of 1901 no source reached in this pass dates a further work, commission, exhibition, address, or event before the death record of 1934. Neither en, fr, nor de.wikipedia, nor Wikidata Q2178796, nor the Wikimedia Commons category fills those thirty-three years. The year 1905 is a marker inside the silence and attests nothing whatever.
stops.campa: The poster boom ends with the century and the sources end with it. Art Nouveau goes out of fashion inside a decade; the collectors move on, the reviews fold, and the men who drew the stems are working for houses that no longer want stems. Where Berthon goes, what he prints, whether he teaches, whether he sells: none of it is written down in anything reachable. Thirty-three years of a man's life sit here with nothing in them at all except the certainty that they happened to him.
suggested_refs: Annuaires, exhibition catalogues, and Sceaux local records, unexamined for the years 1901 to 1934
sources: Absence across en, fr, and de.wikipedia, Wikidata Q2178796, and Wikimedia Commons

stops.name: Sceaux, the house south of Paris
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The death record places him at his own home in Sceaux in February 1934, so he was living there by then; nothing establishes when he moved, and 1930 is a placeholder. No address within the commune has been recovered from any source reached.
stops.campa: At some point he leaves Paris for the small town on its southern edge, a place of gardens and a park and a good railway line, where men from the capital go to be quiet. He is in his fifties or his sixties. The archive says only that when he dies the address is his own house at Sceaux, and nothing about the rooms, or the work on the walls, or whether anyone still came out to see the old designer of flowered posters that the nineteen-twenties had long since made look like another era's furniture.
suggested_refs: Sceaux, Hauts-de-Seine, address within the commune unrecovered
sources: Archives des Hauts-de-Seine, Sceaux, acte de deces n. 23, annee 1934 (via fr.wikipedia wikitext)

stops.name: Sceaux, the twenty-seventh of February
stops.date_confidence: Attested by primary record. Archives des Hauts-de-Seine, commune de Sceaux, acte de deces number 23, annee 1934, vue 6 of 26, cited in fr.wikipedia's wikitext; Wikidata Q2178796 sources the same date to the death certificate and to the BnF authority file, whose heading reads Paul Berthon 1872-1934. He was sixty-one. en.wikipedia's 15 February 1909 is treated at the following stops as an identified error and not as an open contradiction.
stops.campa: He dies at home on the twenty-seventh of February, sixty-one years old, and the mayor's office enters him as act number twenty-three of the year. That number is the firmest thing in his biography. Everything else wobbles between one catalogue and another: the dates on the plates, the year of the violin lesson, the name of a wife. The register of Sceaux does not wobble. It is also, so far as anything reached here shows, the last document that says where he is.
suggested_refs: Archives des Hauts-de-Seine, Sceaux, acte de deces n. 23, annee 1934, vue 6/26

stops.name: Sceaux, the grave that has not been looked for
stops.date_confidence: A gap, stated as a gap. No tomb, cemetery record, or funerary monument for Berthon was located through fr.wikipedia, Wikidata, data.bnf.fr, or the municipal articles for Sceaux and Villefranche-sur-Saone. Search engine access was bot-gated or empty during the research pass and the WebSearch budget was exhausted, so this is an unsearched absence and not evidence that no grave exists. The date is nominal.
stops.campa: Where they put him is not known. A man who died in a Paris suburb in 1934 with a civil act to his name was buried somewhere within a few days, in the communal cemetery or in a family plot back at Villefranche, and the paper that would say which has not been opened by anyone whose work could be reached. The lithographs hang in seven national collections. The grave is a blank, and it is a blank of the ordinary kind, unlooked for rather than lost. No one has yet gone to Sceaux to ask.
suggested_refs: Sceaux communal cemetery registers; Villefranche-sur-Saone family plots. Both unexamined.
sources: Absence across fr.wikipedia, Wikidata, data.bnf.fr, and the municipal articles for Sceaux and Villefranche-sur-Saone

stops.name: Chartrettes, the birth of the man he is mistaken for
stops.date_confidence: Attested by fr.wikipedia's article on Paul Emile Berton: born 4 May 1846 at Chartrettes, Seine-et-Marne. This is a different man, twenty-six years older, and the stop is placed because his life has repeatedly been written into Berthon's, including in the Wikidata description string that puts Chartrettes down as Berthon's birthplace. Coordinates are the commune of Chartrettes.
stops.campa: Twenty-six years before Berthon, in a village on the Seine below Melun, a painter is born named Paul Emile Berton. One letter apart. The two will never meet in any document; they meet everywhere else. Berton's birthplace will be printed as Berthon's in a database description, Berton's lithographs and Berthon's will be swapped on the market, and in the end Berton's death will be handed to Berthon in the English-reading world and left standing there for years.
suggested_refs: fr.wikipedia, 'Paul Emile Berton', born Chartrettes 4 May 1846

stops.name: Paris, the sixteenth arrondissement, a death borrowed
stops.date_confidence: Attested for Berton and misapplied to Berthon. Paul Emile Berton died on 15 February 1909 in the sixteenth arrondissement of Paris; en.wikipedia gives exactly that day, month, city, and year as the death of Paul Berthon and puts his age at 36. Berthon was alive and had twenty-five years left. Both French articles now carry hatnotes warning against the confusion. Coordinates are the sixteenth arrondissement generally, not an address.
stops.campa: On this day a painter dies in the sixteenth arrondissement, and the record of it goes wandering. It fastens onto a lithographer who is at that moment thirty-six years old and working. English Wikipedia carries the borrowed death to this day; the Cleveland Museum of Art still prints the dates 1872 to 1909 under a Berthon on its wall. Both French articles open with a warning notice against the confusion, and that notice is the only monument the two men have in common.
stops.quote: Il est parfois confondu avec le lithographe français Paul Berthon (1872-1934)
suggested_refs: The Confusion hatnotes on fr.wikipedia's Berthon and Berton articles
clevelandart.org/art/1991.175, labelled French, 1872-1909

stops.name: Paris, Pere-Lachaise, division 29
stops.date_confidence: Attested for Berton: buried at Pere-Lachaise, division 29, per fr.wikipedia. The burial date is a placeholder within the days after his death on 15 February 1909. This is not Berthon's grave; the stop records where the misattributed death leads a reader. Coordinates approximate division 29 of the cemetery.
stops.campa: Berton goes into division twenty-nine and stays there, marked, findable, visited. It is the grave a reader arrives at who follows the English encyclopedia's dates for Berthon to their end. The man actually named in that entry has no located grave at all. The one with the stone is the one who did not draw the pictures, and the market completes the exchange in the other direction, selling Berthon's lithographs under Berton's name to buyers who have no way of telling them apart.
suggested_refs: Pere-Lachaise, division 29, grave of Paul Emile Berton

stops.name: New York, the sheets in the museums
stops.date_confidence: Holdings attested by Wikidata Q2178796, statement P6379: the Museum of Modern Art, the National Gallery of Art, the National Gallery of Victoria, the Nelson-Atkins Museum of Art, the National Gallery of Canada, the National Museum Paleis Het Loo, and the Stedelijk Museum. No acquisition dates were established for any of them; 1960 is a nominal marker for a process spread across decades. Coordinates are the Museum of Modern Art.
stops.campa: The panels end where he never went. New York, Washington, Melbourne, Kansas City, Ottawa, Amsterdam, Apeldoorn: seven collections on four continents hold sheets that were pulled a hundred at a time on presses in the ninth arrondissement, to be sold cheap and pinned up in rooms where nobody could afford a painting. The cheapness was the whole point of them. Being kept flat in solander boxes by curators is the exact fate the decorative panel was invented to avoid, and it is the only reason any survive.
suggested_refs: Wikidata Q2178796, statement P6379, collections holding Berthon's work

stops.name: Paris, Arwas puts the pupil beside the master
stops.date_confidence: Attested by fr.wikipedia's bibliography: Victor Arwas, Berthon and Grasset, Academy Editions and Denoel, 1978. The month is unknown. The book itself was not read for this pass; only the bibliographic entry was reached. Coordinates are the canonical Paris anchor, though the volume was published in London and Paris both.
stops.campa: Forty-four years after his death a book puts his name on a cover next to the man who taught him decorative composition on the rue Vavin. That is the shape his recovery takes: not a monograph of his own but a joint one, the pupil admitted in the master's company. Gerald Schurr will file him the following year among the petits maitres of French painting, in a series whose entire purpose is to bring back the men the big histories left out. Both books treat him as somebody who needs bringing back.
suggested_refs: Victor Arwas, Berthon and Grasset, Academy Editions and Denoel, 1978
Gerald Schurr, Les Petits Maitres de la peinture 1820-1920, vol. IV, 1979

stops.name: Paris, the authority file that settles the dates
stops.date_confidence: The BnF authority record ark:/12148/cb14958722g is headed Paul Berthon 1872-1934 and is cited by Wikidata as a source for the death date. No creation date for the record was established and 1990 is a nominal marker, not an attested year. Coordinates are the canonical Paris anchor rather than a library building.
stops.campa: A cataloguer at the national library writes the two dates on a card, and the card becomes a number, and the number is what every other library in the world will copy. 1872 to 1934. It agrees with the register at Sceaux and with the civil act in the fifth arrondissement, and it disagrees with the museum labels and the dealers' catalogues that go on selling him as a man who died young. The correction exists and has existed for years. Whether the trade adopts it is a separate question, and the answer so far is no.
suggested_refs: BnF authority record ark:/12148/cb14958722g, Paul Berthon (1872-1934)

stops.name: Paris, place de la Madeleine, the decorative revolution
stops.date_confidence: Attested by fr.wikipedia's bibliography: L'Art Nouveau, la Revolution decorative, Pinacotheque de Paris and Skira, 2013, an exhibition catalogue co-authored by Victor Arwas. The months of the exhibition were not established. Coordinates are the Pinacotheque de Paris at 28 place de la Madeleine, supplied here rather than taken from the source, and are reconstruction.
stops.campa: A century after the stems went out of fashion the movement comes back to a private gallery on the place de la Madeleine, under a title that calls it a revolution, and Berthon is inside the catalogue. Victor Arwas, who had put his name beside Grasset's on a cover thirty-five years earlier, is one of the authors. The recovery of a minor master runs through very few hands, and this one runs through his. A name stays findable as long as somebody keeps writing it down, and stops when he stops.
suggested_refs: L'Art Nouveau, la Revolution decorative, Pinacotheque de Paris and Skira, 2013

stops.name: Paris, the question that was never answered
stops.date_confidence: Not an event in his life. This stop records the state of an open research question on the date of compilation. The atlas queue flagged an unconfirmed Argentina connection for Berthon; the research pass found no mention of Argentina, Buenos Aires, or Latin America in en, fr, or de.wikipedia, Wikidata Q2178796, the Wikimedia Commons category, archive.org search, or the Cleveland Museum catalogue entry. But the WebSearch budget was exhausted before the pass began, Gallica's endpoint returned 403, and the search engines were bot-gated, so the negative is partial. The Buenos Aires pin is deliberately not placed.
stops.campa: Somebody, at some point, wrote down that this man had something to do with Argentina, and no page that can be opened says why. The encyclopedias in three languages do not mention it. Neither does the database, and neither does the one museum catalogue that carries his name. That silence is not an answer, because the newspapers and trade journals where such a trace would sit were never reached, and the search that produced the silence was cut short. The question stands open where it was found.
